cf.title: Hash index inserts serialise on the metapage tuple counter

input.subject: Hash index inserts serialise on the metapage tuple counter

verdict_reasoning: The problem is stated and measured, and the one reviewer supports fixing it, so level 1 holds. The design has open points at level 2. Counts lost at backend exit add up on insert-only indexes with nothing to recount them (replication-ondisk-1). v2 brought batching back, so split timing again depends on client count and session length, and David Geier's objection has no answer (maintenance-fit-1). The list should settle these before code review.

brief.title: Stop hash index inserts from serializing on the metapage lock
brief.problem: Every hash index insert takes the metapage's exclusive content lock to bump hashm_ntuples and test the split threshold. With concurrent inserters this one buffer serializes them, so single-row insert throughput peaks at 16 clients and falls, while btree keeps scaling. In a growing index, overflow page allocation and free also lock the metapage and the bitmap page.
brief.proposed_design: 0001: an insert that finds the metapage lock taken does not wait; it keeps the tuple as a pending count in a backend-local hash table keyed by index OID, flushed by a later insert that gets the lock. After 1024 inserts and contention, a backend tries only every 32nd insert or after adding an overflow page, and waits at 256 pending. 0002 searches bitmap pages under a share lock, extends by 64 overflow pages at once, and frees without the metapage.
user_visible_surface: XLOG_HASH_INSERT changes: the metapage block reference is optional and may carry a tuple count increment; needs an XLOG_PAGE_MAGIC bump.
XLOG_HASH_ADD_OVFL_PAGE gains a page count and registers the metapage only when it changes.
pg_waldump output for hash insert records shows "ntuples +N".
A growing index may hold up to 63 unused overflow pages from the last batch.
author_claims: Without concurrent inserters the count is exact and split timing matches master.
hashm_ntuples only times splits, so a count that lags by under 256 tuples per backend only delays a split.
On 64 vCPUs, single-row inserts reach about 686k tps at 256 clients against 50k on master, level with btree.
Mixed, single-key, delete-heavy and high-duplicate runs give the same buckets and row counts as master, and a standby replays to the same metapage.
Single-client INSERT ... SELECT shows no regression, and WAL per insert drops slightly.
brief.thread_state: David Geier supported fixing the problem and objected to non-deterministic, concurrency-dependent split timing in the first batching design; he has not replied since v1. The author posted v1 to v4 alone, and v4 only fixes tests that failed on cfbot.
unclear: Whether v4's 1024-insert and every-32nd rules still make split timing depend on client count, which was David Geier's main objection.
The thread does not say how the pending-count hash table behaves on index drop, reindex or OID reuse, or on subtransaction abort.
The thread has no measurement of how far hashm_ntuples drifts on insert-only tables where VACUUM never recounts.
Whether the 1024, 32, 256 and 64 constants should be tunable, and how they were chosen beyond one machine.
No reviewer has checked the new 0002 bitmap locking protocol, the cached-metapage refresh rule or the new lock order.

objections.title: Uncounted tuples persist in hashm_ntuples with no repair on insert-only tables
objections.failure_scenario: A pooler recycles backends after a few thousand inserts each, under contention. Each exit drops up to 255 pending tuples per index into the on-disk metapage permanently. On an append-only table VACUUM never recounts, so splits fall further behind, bucket chains lengthen and probes slow. pg_upgrade carries the low count forward.
objections.argument: Message #7 shows that a count far below reality makes _hash_expandtable() refuse splits, so chains grow. The 1.4% worst case in message #8 was for 10-insert sessions; sessions just past the 1024-insert threshold can lose up to 255 of about 1300 tuples. Message #2 notes that VACUUM recounts only when it removes tuples and sees no concurrent split or insert. The proposal offers no recount path for insert-only indexes.
objections.author_must_show: How far does hashm_ntuples drift on an insert-only table when backends exit after about 1100 to 2000 contended inserts, and what corrects it?

critic.reasoning: The 1.4% figure in message #8 covers 10-insert sessions only. No run measures sessions that exit soon after 1024 inserts with up to 255 tuples pending, and message #7 confirms nothing recounts an insert-only index.

objections.title: Hard-coded constants make split timing depend on session length and concurrency
objections.failure_scenario: A user reports that a hash index grew unusually long overflow chains under a pooler with mid-length sessions. A developer cannot reproduce it, because whether a split fires depends on client count, on whether each backend crossed 1024 inserts, and on the every-32nd-insert phase. Nothing logs or exposes the pending counts.
objections.argument: In message #2 David Geier objected that batched counting makes splitting "workload dependent and by that non-deterministic", and in message #4 he asked that any alternative be checked against that problem. v1 met that goal only for uncontended inserts. v2 brought batching back after 1024 inserts, tuned on one 48-core machine (message #8), and the constants 1024, 32, 256 and 64 are fixed. No one has replied to v2 through v4 to say the objection no longer applies.
objections.author_must_show: How would someone debugging a split-timing report find out the current pending counts, and why are 1024, 32 and 256 right on hardware other than the one test machine?

critic.reasoning: v2 brought batching back after 1024 inserts, so split timing under contention again depends on client count and session length. David Geier's objection from messages #2 and #4 has no answer for v2 to v4, and the constants come from one machine.

objections.title: Pending counts keyed by index OID can flow into a new relfilenode
objections.failure_scenario: A backend holds pending counts for an index. Another session runs TRUNCATE or REINDEX, which writes a new metapage with ntuples 0. The first backend's next insert flushes its stale pending count into the new metapage, and a near-empty index then splits early and carries a wrong count until a VACUUM removes tuples.
objections.argument: The commit message keys the backend-local hash table by index OID. TRUNCATE, REINDEX and dropping the index with later OID reuse all keep or reuse that OID with a new relfilenode. The proposal does not say when an entry is discarded: on relcache invalidation, on relfilenode change, or on drop. The brief lists this as unclear, and no reply in the thread covers it.
objections.author_must_show: When is a pending-count entry discarded, so that a count from an old relfilenode can never reach a new metapage?

critic.reasoning: The harm is small, since a stale flush adds fewer than 256 tuples per backend and only causes an early split. But the proposal does not say when an entry keyed by index OID is discarded, and the brief lists this as open.

objections.title: Fixed 64-page overflow batch adds persistent size to small indexes
objections.failure_scenario: A schema has 1000 partitions, each with a small hash index that needs its first overflow page. Each extension adds 64 pages instead of 1, about 504 KiB per index, so about 500 MiB of unused space persists on disk and in base backups. The space is never returned.
objections.argument: Message #9 and the 0002 commit message extend by 64 overflow pages whenever none are free, whatever the index size. The only measurement is one large delete-heavy index, which grew by 41 pages (message #9). Small indexes, which gain nothing from contention relief, pay the same fixed cost.
objections.author_must_show: Could the batch size scale with the index size or the number of existing overflow pages, and what does 0002 add for a hash index with 10k rows?

critic.reasoning: The arithmetic is right and 0002 uses a fixed batch of 64 at any index size. The README says only the last page is written, so file systems with holes may use less disk, but no small-index measurement is shown.

objections.title: No field reports of hash index users hitting this contention
objections.failure_scenario: A committer takes on two WAL record changes, a deferred-count scheme and a new bitmap lock protocol in the hash AM. Few production users run many concurrent single-row inserts into a hash index, so the gain reaches few people. Nobody who knows the area is engaged, so later bugs in split timing or overflow allocation wait for an owner.
objections.argument: All demand in the material comes from the author's own benchmarks, and message #1 says the problem was found while chasing something else. David Geier's +1 in message #2 is the only other voice, and he has not replied since v1. No -general or -bugs report, customer workload or other system's experience is cited. The 10x collapse is real on the benchmark, but it does not show how many users run that workload.
objections.author_must_show: Which real workloads run highly concurrent inserts into hash indexes today, and are there field reports of them hitting this metapage wait?

critic.reasoning: The benchmark shows a real decline past 16 clients, but the material cites no field report or user workload. The point is sharper for 0002, which adds a new locking protocol for a 2-5% gain; this is a show-demand item.

refuted.title: Lost pending counts accumulate in visible counts with no recount
refuted.failure_scenario: An application uses short connections and inserts into an insert-only table with a hash index under contention. Each exiting backend can leave up to 255 tuples uncounted, and plain VACUUM never recounts. Months later, pageinspect's hash_metapage_info() ntuples, VACUUM VERBOSE output and the index reltuples are far below the real row count, and splits lag the same way.
refuted.argument: The README hunk says the error is "bounded by the cap on pending tuples". That bound holds per backend. Lost counts add up across all backends that have exited since the last recount. Message #7 states that a VACUUM which removes no tuples never calls hashbulkdelete, so an insert-only index is never recounted, and the drift is visible wherever hashm_ntuples is shown or copied into pg_class.
refuted.author_must_show: How large does hashm_ntuples drift after many short sessions on an insert-only table, and what puts it back without a deleting VACUUM?

critic.reasoning: Duplicate of replication-ondisk-1, which states the drift with numbers. Also, on an insert-only table VACUUM does not call hashbulkdelete, so it does not copy hashm_ntuples into reltuples in this scenario.

refuted.title: New hash locking protocol has no reviewer who knows the area
refuted.failure_scenario: A future change to hash overflow handling assumes the old rule that hashm_firstfree is never greater than the first free bit. The change compiles and passes tests, but free pages in earlier bitmap pages stay unused until the next extension. Corruption reports would land on a committer who never reviewed 0002.
refuted.argument: 0002 changes what hashm_firstfree means. It also adds a cached-metapage refresh rule and a new lock order, so bitmap pages are searched under a share lock and locked exclusive only to claim a bit. The visible thread has no reply after message #4, and v1 to v4 were posted by the author alone. The hash AM has few active maintainers, and both patches change WAL records, so any mistake is in master for good once a release ships.
refuted.author_must_show: Which committer familiar with hash index WAL and locking has reviewed the 0002 bitmap protocol and the new hashm_firstfree invariant?

critic.reasoning: The scenario is a hypothetical later change that ignores the README, which documents the new hashm_firstfree meaning and lock order. A thread three weeks old without a second reviewer is a committability note and shows no design flaw.

touch_points.label: on-disk format / pg_upgrade
touch_points.reason: hashm_ntuples may stay low on disk, hashm_firstfree changes meaning, and an index may keep up to 63 unused overflow pages.

touch_points.label: WAL / replication / standby
touch_points.reason: XLOG_HASH_INSERT and XLOG_HASH_ADD_OVFL_PAGE change format, and redo applies a tuple count increment.

touch_points.label: catalog changes
touch_points.reason: see objection replication-ondisk-2: Pending counts keyed by index OID can flow into a new relfilenode

touch_points.label: ABI / extension API
touch_points.reason: hash.h and hash_xlog.h change, so external tools that decode hash WAL records must follow.

touch_points.label: backpatchability
touch_points.reason: Both patches change WAL records and need an XLOG_PAGE_MAGIC bump, so they are for master only.

touch_points.label: maintenance burden ("who maintains this in 10 years")
touch_points.reason: The patches add a deferred-count scheme with four fixed constants, a new bitmap lock protocol and a new lock order in the hash AM.

touch_points.label: performance on the hot path
touch_points.reason: 0001 changes _hash_doinsert, which every hash index insert runs.

touch_points.label: doesn't fit what Postgres is about (extension / external tool / already solved)

questions: How far does hashm_ntuples drift on an insert-only table when backends exit after about 1100 to 2000 contended inserts, and what corrects it?
Does split timing in v4 still depend on client count and session length, and if so, why is that acceptable given the objection in message #2?
When is a pending-count entry discarded, so that a count from before TRUNCATE, REINDEX, a drop with OID reuse or a subtransaction abort never reaches a metapage?
What does 0002 add on disk for a hash index with 10k rows, and could the 64-page batch scale with index size?
Which real workloads run many concurrent single-row inserts into hash indexes, and are there field reports of this metapage wait?

committability.owner_note: It needs a committer who knows the hash AM's locking rules and hash WAL replay. None has spoken in the visible thread.
committability.liability: The owner signs for two WAL record changes, a new meaning of hashm_firstfree, a new lock order and an approximate hashm_ntuples, for as long as the hash AM exists.
committability.author_follow_up: The author posted v1 to v4 within three weeks and fixed the cfbot test failures in v4, which suggests he stays for fixes.

priority.reason: The gain is large on the benchmark, but it reaches only users with many concurrent inserters into a hash index, and no field report is cited. The two patches change WAL records and hash AM locking, so review is costly, and the drift and split-timing questions should be settled first.

provisional_note: Without the code, the 0002 bitmap locking protocol, the cached-metapage refresh rule, the redo of the optional metapage reference and the lifetime of pending-count entries could not be checked. Only 3 of 10 messages were visible, so later answers in the thread may be missed.
disclosure: Prepared by an AI harness; treat as a devil's advocate, not a verdict.

precedents_retrieved.title: Flush SLRU counters in checkpointer process
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch makes the checkpointer report SLRU statistics during normal operation instead of only at server shutdown. After review it moved the WAL and SLRU stats reports into pgstat_report_checkpointer(), so they also run from CheckpointWriteDelay().
precedents_retrieved.objection: The patch's new pg_stat_slru test failed on Windows CI in 031_recovery_conflict. The author traced this to a race on have_slrustats and said a more stable version would follow, but none was posted. The entry was then returned with feedback, which message #9 gives as a consensus to prioritise other patches because this one was not in good shape.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
There
are many patches to be reviewed and this one doesn't seem to be in the
best shape, so we have to prioritise.

precedents_retrieved.title: Planning counters in pg_stat_statements
precedents_retrieved.summary: Add planning counters to pg_stat_statements: a count of how many times a statement was planned and the total planning time, recorded through a planner hook alongside the existing execution counters. The patch passed the planning time to the executor through a new PlannedStmt field and had the planner hook bump the existing nesting level counter.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Tom Lane objected to the design: pgss_ExecutorEnd cleared a field in the cached PlannedStmt, which he said amounted to modifying the plan cache. He also questioned whether the planner hook should change nested_level, and he said the approach assumed a near one-to-one relationship between planner and executor calls that does not hold for cases such as prepared statements. He proposed having the planner hook record planning time with its own pgss_store() call. The author found that this needs the query text in the planner, which would mean changing function signatures, and returned the patch with feedback because he did not have time to rework it during the commitfest.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
What we have here is pgss_ExecutorEnd stomping on the plan cache.
I do *not* find that acceptable.

precedents_retrieved.title: Add parallel counters to pg_stat_statements
precedents_retrieved.summary: Add counters to pg_stat_statements that record how many times a statement was planned with parallelism and how many times it ran with parallel workers. A later version instead counted how often a parallel plan ran without any parallel workers.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Julien Rouhaud said the counters cannot tell why a parallel plan ran without workers: the executor disabled parallel mode (!es_use_parallel_mode, as with the JDBC client) or no workers were free. He asked for separate counters for each case and for better column names. Nobody answered this review, and Michael Paquier marked the entry Returned with feedback after the thread had been idle for a few weeks.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
Both situations are different and in my opinion require
different (and specialized) counters to properly handle them.

precedents_retrieved.title: split tablecmds.c
precedents_retrieved.summary: Split src/backend/commands/tablecmds.c, at over 22,000 lines the largest backend source file, into several files by sub-area. The patch moved the partitioning code to tablecmds_partition.c and added tablecmds_internal.h for the tablecmds.c internals the new file needs.
precedents_retrieved.objection: No one objected to the split, and several committers supported it. The patch stopped applying, a reviewer asked for a rebase, and the author replied that he did not know if or when he would return to it, so the entry was withdrawn.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
Unfortunately, I'm not sure if/when I will get back to
this one.

precedents_retrieved.title: Split index and table statistics into different types of stats
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch splits the cumulative statistics kind PGSTAT_KIND_RELATION into PGSTAT_KIND_TABLE and a new PGSTAT_KIND_INDEX, with index-specific counting macros and SQL-callable functions. The goal is sensible field names for index stats and lower memory use, since index entries currently carry unused table counters.
precedents_retrieved.objection: The patch stalled. Review comments from Andres Freund and Melanie Plageman were still open, and the author put the work on hold until the related "Generate pg_stat_get_xact*() functions with Macros" patch was done. After that patch was committed, no new version came; the CFM returned the entry because it no longer applied and tests failed.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
This patch no longer applies (with tests failing when it did), and the thread
has stalled.

precedents_retrieved.title: Split index and table statistics into different types of stats
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch splits the cumulative statistics for indexes and tables into two kinds, PGSTAT_KIND_TABLE and a new PGSTAT_KIND_INDEX, with index-specific counting macros and SQL functions. The goal is sensible field names and lower memory use, since index stats today reuse the table format and leave many fields unused.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Andres Freund objected that the patch makes bufmgr.c aware of the relation kind, and suggested first moving relkind-agnostic counters such as blocks_hit and blocks_fetched into per-relfilenode stats. The author agreed to do the relfilenode stats work first and set the entry to Waiting on Author. Michael Paquier later returned the entry because there was no update since January 2024 and the relfilenode work had been posted separately.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
It's not nice from a layering POV that we need this level of awareness in
bufmgr.c.  I wonder if this is an argument for first splitting out stats like
blocks_hit, blocks_fetched into something like "relfilenode stats" - they're
agnostic of the relkind.

precedents_retrieved.title: introduce optimized linear search functions that return index of matching element
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch adds SIMD linear search functions, pg_lfind8_idx() and pg_lfind8_ge_idx(), that return the index of the first matching byte instead of true/false. It came from the radix tree work for lazy vacuum dead tuple storage, and this version also reworks the simd.h helpers it uses.
precedents_retrieved.objection: John Naylor judged that this level of abstraction is not right for the intended use case, the radix tree for lazy vacuum. He said some of the low-level simd.h improvements would be used later in that work, and he returned the entry with feedback.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
As I mentioned in the radix tree thread, I don't believe this level of
abstraction is appropriate for the intended use case.

precedents_retrieved.title: Logical insert/update/delete WAL records for custom table AMs
precedents_retrieved.summary: Add new WAL records representing a logical insert, update, delete (and later truncate) that do nothing at REDO time and are only processed during logical decoding, so that custom table AMs such as a columnar extension can support logical decoding/replication without extensible WAL. Later versions added SQL functions pg_logical_emit_insert/update/delete/truncate and tests using test_decoding.
precedents_retrieved.objection: The author withdrew the patch, saying that with custom WAL resource managers (his parallel extensible rmgr work) it had become less important to him. Earlier, Amit Kapila questioned whether a common heap-tuple-based format could work for all table AMs, and the patch had stopped applying, but the visible messages show no deciding objection from a reviewer.

roaster_notes.note: No precedent found. [P16] covers contention on the shared dynahash HASHHDR.mutex, which is unrelated to hash index metapage locking, and it has no recorded reason. Message #1 points to the v10 metapage cache work, where inserts were noted to still touch the metapage. The thread reports that as a gap left open, not as a rejected attempt.

The proposal adds no SQL syntax, GUC, catalog object or pg_dump state. The WAL format changes are master-only with an XLOG_PAGE_MAGIC bump, which is normal practice. The remaining user-facing change is the meaning of the stored tuple count.
The WAL format changes need only an XLOG_PAGE_MAGIC bump on master. Standby replay was tested with wal_consistency_checking in message #9, so WAL itself raises no objection.

The proposal has no privilege or exposure aspect. It adds no new privilege, role, SQL function, GUC, view or default. The pending counts are backend-local, at most one small entry per index the backend inserts into. The "ntuples +N" text appears only in pg_waldump, which already needs WAL access. Uncounted tuples left by exiting sessions can delay splits on insert-only tables, but only a user who could already bloat the index can do that, so it is a design question for other angles.
Hot-path cost for non-users looks small, since single-client INSERT ... SELECT showed no regression in message #7. The patch set is split so that 0001 can be committed alone.

No existing feature, setting or extension removes the metapage lock from hash index inserts, and an extension cannot change the internals of a core access method. Switching to btree avoids the bottleneck but does not fix hash indexes, and [P16] concerns dynahash, not hash indexes.
The problem is stated with measurements. The open point is how many users it affects, which only field evidence can settle.
